Early agriculture. Roughly ten thousand to five thousand years ago, humans first cultivated crops and domesticated animals, transforming from hunting and gathering to farming. This transition was one of history's most transformative developments, enabling permanent settlements, population growth, and the emergence of complex societies. Sites like Çatalhöyük and Jericho provide archaeological evidence of these early farming communities. Paradoxically, some scholars argue that farming reduced individual nutrition and leisure time compared to foraging, yet its comparative efficiency supported much larger populations.

This shift emerged independently in multiple regions. The Fertile Crescent developed wheat and barley. China cultivated millet and rice. Mesoamerica grew maize and beans. The Andes also became an independent center of agriculture. These developments required new technologies: grinding stones for grain, storage pits, and irrigation channels. Farmers could not follow herds and thus built villages and towns, creating permanent settlements for the first time. Population growth followed due to a more reliable food supply, though paradoxically with poorer nutrition and health overall.

Agriculture facilitated social stratification. Surplus production allowed some individuals to avoid farming entirely and specialize as priests, warriors, and artisans. It also created property concepts; land became owned and heritable in ways it was not for nomadic peoples. The process was gradual and uneven. Many communities remained foragers or practiced mixed subsistence for centuries. Domestication itself was incremental; early farmers managed wild plants and animals for centuries before achieving full dependence on cultivars.

Trade networks emerged around surplus goods like obsidian, pottery, and shells, linking early agricultural settlements across vast distances. Denser populations created new challenges in disease, sanitation, and resource management that shaped emerging social structures. Agriculture transformed human civilization through these interconnected developments.
